newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Dec 3.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Dec 3.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A continued rise in the Australian dollar - which yesterday broke through US82 cents to hit a six-year high - coupled with figures released yesterday which revealed sluggish retail sales, slumping house-building approvals and a build-up of unsold goods, offered fresh signs that the economy remains weak. Page 1.

The continuation of aerial rollouts for major telecommunications companies Telstra and Optus was yesterday given conditional support by the Coalition, who argue there are solid economic and technical reasons why the rollout should continue, disappointing local government representatives who had hoped to see the companies forced to stop the rollout of cables by July 1, 1997 unless agreements had been made with local councils. Page 2.

Prime Minister John Howard has reiterated his desire to serve a full term in Parliament and has threatened to "do what is necessary" in order to get the Coalition's program through the Senate after a series of obstructions, but also said he was willing to be flexible to find common ground with the Upper House to secure his agenda. Page 3.

A claim over all the undeveloped crown land in Darwin announced by the Larrakia Aboriginal people, but not yet lodged with the Native Title Tribunal, has been described as "extravagant" or "ambit" and could undermine support for the native title process, according to Prime Minister John Howard. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

As the Australian dollar continued on its record-breaking path to reach a six-year high of US82 cents yesterday - the US3 cent surge in the past three weeks has seen the local currency reach levels not seen since late 1990 - there were renewed fears about the viability of manufacturing and fresh calls for another interest rate cut. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard went on the offensive yesterday over claims from News Limited executive chairman Ken Cowley that he was using the Senate as a scapegoat for failing to implement key economic reforms, telling ABC radio the Government had been able to implement most of its reform agenda in the past nine months despite an obstructionist Senate. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday struck back at "domestic and expatriate" republican critics, including expatriate writer Robert Hughes, saying they would be proved wrong when the Government unveiled its plan for a people's convention to consider a republic, and branding them "self-appointed dietitians" on what was best for Australia. Page 1.

Figures released yesterday by research company AC Nielsen show that, despite success with the Atlanta Olympics and the growth of Australian Rules football, the Seven Network failed to snatch the lion's share of national ratings from the Nine Network this year, with Nine winning the prime-time ratings for the sixteenth consecutive year despite slipping 0.4 per cent to 31.9 per cent. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

A new Herald AGB-McNair survey, conducted last weekend, has found a referendum on the republic would meet the constitutional test for change, winning the backing of voters in a majority of States, with all States except Tasmania now having majority republican support. Page 1.

The New South Wales Government is facing strong opposition from ethnic community leaders and MPs over claims made by Police Commissioner Peter Ryan during a wide-ranging interview with British trade magazine Police Review last week, that crime in New South Wales is "horrific", with strong links to ethnic groups. Page 1.

After the Australian dollar surged to US82 cents yesterday for the first time since October 1990, chances of another cut to interest rates improved, with research from National Mutual also suggesting that the inflation rate will fall below one per cent in the next year. Page 1.

The National Council of Churches in Australia, which includes the Anglican Church of Australia, the Catholic Church, the Antiochian Church and the Salvation Army, has compared the forcible separation of Aboriginal children from their parents to a Nazi atrocity and has demanded a national non-partisan apology. Page 3.
THE AGE

Security has been tightened at the Australian embassy in Phnom Penh after warnings by the Cambodian Government that diplomats at the Australian, French, United States and Vietnamese embassies have been identified as possible targets. However, no indication was given of who might be behind the attacks. Page A1.

Victoria Legal Aid managing director Robert Cornall claims directors are considering a cut to legal aid services for committals in the Magistrates Court on 18 December, a move which may see defendants having to represent themselves in criminal hearings. Cornall says a strategy is necessary to deal with Federal cuts which will reduce the 1997-98 Victorian budget to A$67 million. Page A1.

Australian Securities Commission records have revealed that John Dahlsen, one of three men appointed to review the office of Victoria's auditor-general, was a director of Sandridge City Development Company which was involved in the previous Labor Government's aborted A$700 million Bayside development in 1992 and the subject of a critical report by the auditor-general four years ago. Page A1.

Figures released yesterday by the Australian Bureau of Statistics reveal that while sales in the rest of Australia dwindled in the lead up to Christmas, Victoria recorded annual growth of 6.3 per cent in the areas of food, clothing and household goods. Pae A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
